questionStem: Five minutes after delivery, a full-term newborn shows peripheral cyanosis, decreased muscle tone, and decreased reflex activity. His pulse is 80/min, and respirations are irregular. Which of the following is the most likely Apgar score?
correctExplanation: Apgar scoring is performed at 1 and 5 minutes after birth to assess the status of the newborn and need for possible resuscitation. The Apgar score consists of points given in five different categories (appearance, pulse, grimace or reflex irritability, activity/muscle tone, and respiratory effort) summed together to compute the Apgar score. Each category is given 0, 1, or 2 points, with 0 points for absent function, 1 for diminished or irregular function, and 2 for a normal, expected presentation. Newborns with lower scores, especially below 7, may require further evaluation and/or intervention. This patient would receive a score of 1 for peripheral cyanosis, 1 for decreased muscle tone, 1 for decreased reflex activity, 1 for pulse less than 100/min, and 1 for irregular respirations, totaling an Apgar score of 5. This indicates the potential need for further resuscitation. Apgar scores are not necessarily associated with later functional or developmental abnormalities.

correctExplanation: Bicuspid aortic valves may be inherited or sporadic. As a result of their geometry and abnormal leaflet excursion, they are subject to more blood flow turbulence (generating the murmur) and shear forces. questionStem: A3-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of pale complexion, low-grade fever, vomiting, occasional diarrhea, and poor feeding. On arrival, he appears mildly dehydrated and cyanotic. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 165/min, respirations are 35/min, and blood pressure is 80/48 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 85%. A grade 3/6, harsh systolic ejection murmur is heard over the entire precordium. Perfusion and muscle tone are normal. During attempts to insert an intravenous catheter, the patient begins to cry and becomes agitated. His oxygen saturation decreases to 60%, and the murmur becomes barely audible. Supplemental oxygen is administered. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Tetralogy of Fallot is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with paroxysmal cyanosis during crying spells and a 3/6 systolic ejection murmur on examination. Tetralogy of Fallot consists of pulmonary infundibular stenosis, overriding aorta, ventricular septal defect (VSD), and right ventricular hypertrophy, resulting in a right- to-left shunt with cyanosis first noted in infancy. Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction eventually leads to right ventricular hypertrophy. The murmur heard with Tetralogy of Fallot, which is typically a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border, is caused by RVOT obstruction, not as often by the VSD. Paroxysmal cyanosis that occurs during periods of crying is a classic presentation and these episodes are referred to as “tet” spells. Patients during one of these spells often exhibit rapid, deep breathing, agitation, and progressive cyanosis. These periods of cyanosis occur as a result of transient obstruction or occlusion of the RVOT leading to decreased blood flow through the pulmonary circulation, although the cause of the underlying transient obstruction is unclear. Treatment of tetralogy of Fallot is with surgical correction. Surgery aims to relieve the RVOT obstruction, close the VSD, and separate the pulmonary and systemic circulation. questionStem: A5-day-old boy of Mediterranean descent is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of progressive jaundice. He has had five yellow, seedy stools daily during this period. He was born at term to a 32-year-old primigravid woman. During the third trimester, his mother took an old prescription of sulfamethoxazole for cystitis without consulting the physician. The blood group of the mother and the newborn is O, Rh-positive. He receives 2 ounces of a cow's milk-based formula every 2 hours. Examination shows no abnormalities except for jaundice from the head to the upper thighs. His hematocrit is 33%, and total serum bilirubin concentration is 20 mg/dL with a direct component of 0.9 mg/dL. Direct and indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) tests are negative. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's jaundice?
correctExplanation: Neonatal jaundice is defined as an increased bilirubin (>5 mg/dL) that results from either increased hemolysis (bilirubin generation) or decreased bilirubin conjugation or excretion. Hyperbilirubinemia can be divided into direct and indirect forms in which either conjugated or unconjugated bilirubin accumulate, respectively. It can also be divided into physiologic and pathologic forms. This patient has anemia and an indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia that has presented in the first few days of life, suggesting a pathologic hemolytic process. The differential includes immune-mediated hemolysis, inherited erythrocyte membrane defects, and erythrocyte enzyme deficiencies. For this patient with a negative Coombs test and Mediterranean background, the most likely cause of his unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia is deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD). G6PD is an enzyme in erythrocytes that makes NADPH from NADP+. An inadequate supply of NADPH leads to decreased concentrations of glutathione, which is a critical scavenger of reactive oxygen species within erythrocytes. Increased oxidative stress, which can occur with exposure to sulfa-containing compounds, results in hemolysis. . questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of dark-colored urine for 5 days and a facial rash for 1 day. She has a history of diffuse joint pain treated with acetaminophen. Her blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. She appears pale and thin. Examination shows a prominent, erythematous, butterfly- shaped macular eruption over the face. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely to be decreased?
correctExplanation: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disorder with a wide range of presentations. Cutaneous manifestations include an erythematous rash over the malar cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds after sun exposure or discoid lesions with hyperpigmented edges and pink, atrophic centers. Painless oral ulcers and nonspecific hair loss may also occur. Fatigue, joint pain, and fever are also common presenting signs. Lupus nephritis is a common complication of SLE, particularly in younger women. Patients with lupus nephritis typically present with evidence of active SLE and may additionally display oliguria or anuria, signs and symptoms of hypertension (eg, headache, visual disturbance), uremia (eg, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pruritus, altered mental status), hyperkalemia (eg, peaked T waves on ECG), and hypervolemia with peripheral edema. Lupus nephritis involves glomerular deposition of antibodies, including IgG, IgM, and IgA, as well as activation of the classical complement pathway. Laboratory studies therefore generally show hypocomplementemia with decreased serum concentrations of early classical pathway components such as C1q, C2, C3, C4, and CHS50, as well as increased creatinine. Kidney biopsy is useful for disease staging and may show a range of histologic patterns from mesangial glomerulonephritis to diffuse proliferative or membranous glomerulonephritis.

It is often triggered by an allergen (eg, smoke, pollen), exercise, or temperature change. In the case of allergen-induced asthma, bronchoconstriction is triggered by IgE-mediated activation of mast cells, followed by degranulation and histamine release. Such mast cell activation is classified as a type | hypersensitivity reaction. These reactions are composed of two phases, the immediate and the late phase. In the immediate phase, preformed IgE on the surface of mast cells and basophils is crosslinked by an antigen leading to their degranulation and release of histamine, which results in vasodilation, vascular permeability, and bronchoconstriction among other effects. The late phase occurs hours after the initial insult and is mediated by the release of prostaglandins and leukotrienes synthesized by the mast cells. Treatment for asthma depends on the classification (intermittent, mild/moderate/severe persistent). To diagnose Kawasaki disease, fever for 5 days or more plus four of the remaining criteria are required. Laboratory studies may show thrombocytosis and increased ESR. questionStem: An asymptomatic 17-year-old boy comes to the physician for a routine examination prior to participation in school sports. Examination shows no is abnormalities except for approximately 10 light brown hyperpigmented lesions over the trunk and extremities; the lesions vary in size from 0.6 to 2 cm in diameter. There are also some freckle-like lesions over both axillae. Compared to the general population, this patient is at increased risk for which of the following?
correctExplanation: Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder (phakomatosis) that typically results from an inherited mutation of the NF1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17. NF7 is inherited with complete penetrance and variable expressivity. Rarely, the mutation in the NF1 gene occurs sporadically. NF1 presents with cutaneous neurofibromas (benign neoplasms derived from neural crest cells), plexiform neurofibromas, hyperpigmented maculae, axillary or inguinal freckling, pigmented iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), cognitive disability, and seizures. Patients with NF1 are at increased risk for optic nerve glioma and pheochromocytoma. Optic nerve gliomas are typically indolent lesions and are most frequently low-grade pilocytic astrocytomas. The lesion may involve one or both optic nerves or the optic chiasm. Affected patients present with insidious vision loss, proptosis, and optic nerve atrophy. correctExplanation: Gastroesophageal reflux disease is extremely common in infants. This is the result of diminished closing pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter, permitting acidic contents of the stomach to reflux into the esophagus. Reflux events may occur up to 30 times per day. Some of these episodes result in contents entering the oral cavity and decrease through the first year of life. Infants who demonstrate good weight gain, are feeding well, and are not irritable, are managed conservatively. Modifications that may improve symptoms include having infants avoid secondhand smoke exposure, smaller and more frequent meals, and keeping infants upright after feeding when possible. Infants who experience reflux and poor weight gain should undergo further evaluation for calorie count, ultrasonography to rule out pyloric stenosis, and have their diets adjusted to thickened feeds or breast milk.
